name: Latin American Folk Saints
dom: Vernacular sanctity, popular canonization, miraculous intercession
note: Hub for the folk-canonized (popular, Rome-unrecognized) intercessory figures of modern Latin American vernacular Catholicism; well attested ethnographically.

name: Santa Muerte
dom: Death personified, protection, healing, justice, love, devotion of the marginalized
note: Mexican folk 'saint' (Holy Death), a skeletal female personification of death venerated since at least the mid-20th c. with mass public shrines (Tepito); not recognized by Rome; imagery descends from the personified Grim Reaper / Death.

name: San La Muerte
dom: Death personified, protection, oaths, sudden help
note: Argentine/Paraguayan/Guaraní-zone male folk saint of personified Death (skeletal figure); publicly venerated in the Litoral region; Rome-unrecognized; cognate of the broader Death-saint devotion.

name: Maximón (San Simón)
dom: Fortune, fertility, protection, intercession, bargains and vows, Maya-Catholic intercession
note: Guatemalan Maya-Catholic syncretic figure of the highlands (esp. Santiago Atitlán, San Andrés Itzapa), publicly identified with St. Simon and an Indigenous Maya ancestral/Mam figure; an effigy receives offerings of tobacco and liquor. Only the public devotion is modeled.

name: Jesús Malverde
dom: Protection of the poor and travelers, intercession, popular justice
note: Sinaloan (Mexico) folk saint, said to be an early-20th-c. bandit-benefactor executed c.1909; venerated at a Culiacán chapel; not recognized by Rome. Modeled neutrally as a publicly attested devotion.

name: Niño Fidencio
note: José Fidencio Constantino Síntora (1898–1938), a celebrated curandero of Espinazo, Nuevo León (Mexico); posthumously venerated as a folk healer-saint with a living devotional movement (fidencistas); Rome-unrecognized.

name: Sarita Colonia
dom: Protection of migrants, the poor and the marginalized, intercession
note: Sara Colonia Zambrano (1914–1940), a poor migrant woman in Callao, Peru; posthumously venerated as a folk saint of the urban marginalized; Rome-unrecognized.

name: Difunta Correa
dom: Protection of travelers and the desperate, miraculous nourishment, intercession
note: Argentine folk saint (Deolinda Correa), a 19th-c. woman said to have died of thirst in the San Juan desert while her nursing infant survived; major roadside shrine at Vallecito; Rome-unrecognized.

name: San Pascualito
dom: Death personified, healing, protection from epidemic, intercession
note: Guatemalan/Chiapas Maya-Catholic skeletal folk saint of Death, publicly associated by name with the canonical St. Paschal Baylón but venerated as a personified-Death figure; centered at Olintepeque and Chiapas; Rome-unrecognized in this form.
